title: The Cricket on the Hearth
author: Charles Dickens
setting: A carrier's cottage and the small town along his round, somewhere in rural England, over three days at the end of January
lengthNote: Three Chirps, around 31,000 words, a little longer than A Christmas Carol
openingLine: The kettle began it! Don't tell me what Mrs. Peerybingle said.
summary: A carrier brings home an old deaf passenger he found by the roadside, and his young wife cries out when the stranger comes near the fire. Two days later a toy merchant shows him, through a counting-house window, the same man without his white wig and with an arm round her waist. John Peerybingle spends the night between a loaded gun and his own hearth, and by morning blames himself for the marriage. Beside this, a poor toymaker has spent years describing a comfortable house and a kind employer to his blind daughter, and both fictions come apart on the same wedding morning.
referenceStyle: chirp — Dickens divides the book into three Chirps, and references name the Chirp

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Cricket on the Hearth (eBook 20795)
sourceText.note: Transcribed from an American illustrated edition of 1905 (New York: Platt & Peck), the text the book page links to. It prints the three Chirps complete but leaves out Dickens's dedication to Lord Jeffrey, which is described here from the 1846 Bradbury and Evans printing. Quotations follow the transcription's wording and spelling, with its double hyphens set as dashes.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Bradbury and Evans issued it shortly before Christmas as The Cricket on the Hearth. A Fairy Tale of Home, with 1846 on the title page.

atAGlance.label: Place in the series
atAGlance.note: The third of Dickens's Christmas books, after A Christmas Carol and The Chimes, and before The Battle of Life and The Haunted Man.

atAGlance.label: Illustrators
atAGlance.note: Daniel Maclise, Richard Doyle, John Leech, Clarkson Stanfield and Edwin Landseer, whose single plate is of Boxer the dog.

atAGlance.label: Time span
atAGlance.note: The story ends on the last day of the first month, which is Tackleton's wedding day and the Peerybingles' first wedding anniversary.

structure.label: Chirp the First
structure.title: A kettle, a cricket and a passenger left till called for
structure.summary: An evening at the Peerybingles' fireside is built out of sounds before anyone speaks: kettle, Dutch clock and cricket compete while Dot waits for John's cart. John brings home parcels, a wedding cake for Tackleton and an old man he found sitting by the roadside. When the stranger comes near the fire Dot cries out and falls into laughing and weeping, and John's evening ends in a vision of Dots at every age, with one young man at her stool who does not belong there.

scenes.summary: The narrator argues that the kettle started first, and the two sing a race until their song reaches John coming down the lane.
Dot finds Tackleton's wedding cake among the parcels, falls silent, and the cricket stops.
A white-haired passenger with a stick that folds into a chair asks to be left till called for, and quizzes John about his 'very young' wife.
Tackleton says the two couples are just alike, asks John whether his wife truly dotes on him, and says he kills crickets.
While Dot fills his pipe, the Cricket calls up a lifetime of Dots for John, and a young man's figure at her stool repeats that she married someone else.

structure.label: Chirp the Second: Caleb's house
structure.title: Caleb’s house, and the one he describes to Bertha
structure.summary: The narrator admits that Caleb and his blind daughter live in two different houses: the cracked wooden shed stuck to Tackleton's premises, and the comfortable home Caleb has described to Bertha for years. Tackleton calls to announce that he is marrying May Fielding and invites himself to Dot's picnic. Bertha takes the news quietly, then asks her father to be her eyes, and questions him about May and about the kind benefactor she believes Tackleton to be.

scenes.summary: Dolls sorted by class from wax to matchsticks, Noah's arks with knockers, and figures that do foolish things when a handle is turned.
Caleb describes his sackcloth coat to Bertha as a fashionable bright blue one, and walks with a light step he has practised for her ear.
Tackleton calls Bertha an idiot under his breath, takes her thanks for a rose-tree Caleb bought, and announces his marriage.
She asks Caleb to describe the room, May and their benefactor, and weeps on his shoulder.

structure.label: Chirp the Second: the picnic
structure.title: A picnic, a confession and a lit window
structure.summary: The Peerybingles drive through the January fog to their fortnightly picnic at Caleb's, where May, her mother and Tackleton have arrived. Dot's talk of the husbands they chose at school brings May to tears, and once John has driven on, Bertha falls at May's feet and confesses that the coming marriage has almost broken her heart. In the evening John returns with the old stranger, and Tackleton takes him across a dark yard to a window through which he sees Dot fixing the stranger's white hair back on a young man's head.

scenes.summary: Boxer runs ahead, every house has a parcel or a greeting, and John is proud to have his wife admired from the cart.
May's mother mentions the Indigo Trade and says the marriages with least love in them are the happiest.
Bertha blesses May and admits her grief, and Caleb understands at one blow what his inventions have done.
Tackleton warns John against violence, then shows him Dot and the stranger in the lamplit ware-room.

structure.label: Chirp the Third: the night
structure.title: A gun, a cricket and a night of thinking
structure.summary: Alone by his cold hearth at ten o'clock, John takes a loaded gun from the wall and goes to the stranger's door. The cricket chirps, he puts the gun aside, and the Cricket appears in fairy shape with the Household Fairies, who show him Dot's conduct in a glass all night. In the morning the stranger is gone through an open window, and John tells Tackleton that Dot is innocent of everything except concealment, that he never considered her enough, and that he will send her home to her parents.

scenes.summary: Rage grows until John raises the gun to beat in the door, and the fire flares as the cricket begins.
The Cricket repeats Dot's words about loving it, corrects John's past tense, and calls the hearth the altar of his home.
Household Fairies show Dot turning down a dance, caring for Bertha and weeping on her stool, and rub out the stranger’s shadow whenever it falls.
John says he took a young woman from her friends to a dull house and will release her with his blessing; Dot overhears.

structure.label: Chirp the Third: the wedding morning
structure.title: Edward Plummer returns, and everything is explained
structure.summary: Caleb brings Bertha to the Carrier's house and tells her the truth about their home and their master, and Dot, asked what she sees, describes Caleb as he really is. Wheels are heard, Edward Plummer comes in without his disguise, and Dot explains that she kept his secret so that he could marry May, which he did at church that morning. Tackleton throws his ring in the fire, then sends the cake and toys to the celebration and comes himself. The book ends with a dance, after which the narrator finds himself alone with a cricket and a broken toy.

scenes.summary: Caleb admits the world he described does not exist; Bertha asks Dot to describe her father and calls the answer her sight restored.
Dot covers Caleb's eyes as a sunburnt young man runs in, and the cuckoo strikes twelve.
Speaking of herself as 'she', Dot tells how she carried messages between Edward and May, then asks John not to love her until he has heard it all.
Tackleton asks Tilly to throw his ring in the fire, then sends the wedding cake and asks to join the party.
Everyone dances, including Tackleton with Mrs Fielding, and then the whole company vanishes from the narrator's sight.

characters.name: John Peerybingle
characters.summary: A slow, heavy, good-natured carrier who is always very near a joke and never gets to it. Dickens gives him the book's hardest night: shown what looks like proof of his wife's betrayal, he reaches for a gun, puts it down when the cricket chirps, and by morning has turned the charge on himself for marrying a woman so much younger.
characters.clue: He takes a loaded gun to a lodger's door at night, and in the morning offers to send his wife back to her parents with his blessing.

relationships.label: more a father than a friend to

characters.name: Dot Peerybingle
characters.summary: Mary Peerybingle, called Dot by her husband, is quick, domestic and good at managing other people's feelings. For most of the book the narrator lets her behave like a guilty wife and even tells the reader they may learn to hate her. Her secret turns out to be a kindness to May and Edward, and her last speech answers the fear she voiced in the first Chirp about an ill-assorted marriage.
characters.clue: She fills her husband's pipe better than anyone in the world, bungles it with Tackleton watching, and asks John to say nothing is over until the clock strikes.

characters.name: Caleb Plummer
characters.role: A poor toymaker working for Gruff and Tackleton
characters.summary: A little, meagre man in a coat made from sacking with the firm's initials stencilled on the back, who has spent years describing that coat to his blind daughter as bright blue. His lies are all kindnesses, and Dickens lets them do damage: Bertha falls in love with the generous master Caleb invented, and her father is left asking whether he deceived her from her cradle only to break her heart.
characters.clue: His greatcoat says G & T and GLASS on the back, he walks with a light step he does not feel, and he falls back on a drinking song whenever a question gets too close.

characters.name: Bertha Plummer
characters.role: Caleb's blind daughter, a doll's dressmaker
characters.summary: She lives in the comfortable house her father describes and loves the kind benefactor he has made out of their employer. Dickens gives her the sharpest ear in the book, since she hears a young man's tread behind the old stranger's disguise. When the truth comes she takes it as a gain, holding her father's grey head and saying she is not blind any longer.
characters.clue: She asks for her patient, willing eyes, hears the step behind a disguise, and falls at a bride's feet.

characters.name: Tackleton
characters.role: Toy merchant, trading as Gruff and Tackleton
characters.summary: A man who despises toys and makes his living from them, adding grim faces and goblins to his stock to frighten children. He is about to marry May Fielding, a much younger woman, and says obedience will be enough for him. He also sets out to show that John's marriage is no better than his own. His change at the end is quick: he sends his wedding cake to the party and asks to be let in because there is no cricket left on his hearth.
characters.clue: One eye is always half shut, he would kill every cricket he hears, and he ends the book sending his own wedding cake to somebody else's party.

characters.name: Edward Plummer
characters.role: Caleb's son, back from South America
characters.summary: Believed dead in what Caleb calls the Golden South Americas, he comes home to hear that his sweetheart is about to marry a wealthier man, and disguises himself as a deaf old man so that he can watch her without being known. He explains the disguise himself in the last Chirp, and his only defence is that John never used to judge a man unheard.
characters.clue: He rides in a carrier's cart as a deaf old man whose walking-stick turns into a chair.

characters.name: May Fielding
characters.summary: Pretty, quiet and almost silent, May has been persuaded by her mother into an engagement she had for some time refused. She says little at the picnic, but her colour and her tears at Dot's talk of school-day sweethearts tell the reader what she will not say. She marries Edward on the morning she was due at church with Tackleton.
characters.clue: Tears come into her eyes at a joke about the husbands girls choose at school, and she is married before the wedding she was expected at.

characters.name: Tilly Slowboy
characters.summary: A foundling in her early teens, brought up by public charity, who cannot cross a room without knocking the baby's head against something. She repeats scraps of adult talk to the baby with the nouns turned plural, and one of these garbled repetitions is the broken hint about Bertha that Tackleton mentions when he comes to apologise.
characters.clue: She begs 'Ow, if you please, don't!', wears a spencer of no known fashion, and hands the baby round the room like something to drink.

characters.name: Mrs Fielding
characters.summary: A small, peevish old lady who believes her family would have been wealthy but for something in the Indigo Trade that she will not describe. She pushes May towards Tackleton on the principle that marriages with least love in them are the happiest, and when the plan collapses she has to be fetched to the celebration by an expedition.
characters.clue: She comes back again and again to the Indigo Trade, wears a cap as stiff as a mitre, and suspects a wedding cake of being poisoned.

characters.name: The Cricket
characters.role: The cricket on the Peerybingles' hearth
characters.summary: The title character chirps in competition with the kettle, falls silent when Dot is troubled, and starts again just as John lifts the gun. The narrator calls it the Genius of the Carrier's Hearth and Home. In fairy form it speaks to John in Dot's own words and calls up Household Fairies to show him her conduct, and the next morning it appears behind Bertha during Caleb's confession, pointing to her father.
characters.clue: It chirps louder than a kettle, stops when a wedding cake arrives, and quotes a wife's words back to her husband in the middle of the night.

themes.name: Hearth and home
themes.summary: Home in this book is a set of sounds and habits, kettle, clock, pipe and stool, and Dickens shows how quickly the same objects change meaning once John suspects his wife. Tackleton's definition, four walls and a ceiling, is the view the book sets out to disprove.
themes.development: Chirp the First builds the home out of noise; Chirp the Second sets Caleb's invented home beside the real shed; in Chirp the Third the Cricket calls the hearth an altar, Dot calls John's heart her home, and Tackleton admits there is no cricket on his.

themes.name: Age, choice and marriage
themes.summary: Three unequal matches are set side by side: John and Dot, Tackleton and May, and the one Mrs Fielding approves of because it has least love in it. John's decision to release Dot rests on the fear Dot herself voiced in the first Chirp, that a husband more like a guardian might never be loved.
themes.development: Tackleton claims in Chirp the First that the two couples are just alike. Chirp the Third tests the claim, finds it false for the Peerybingles, and lets May out of her match by marrying Edward first.

themes.name: Jealousy
themes.summary: John's jealousy arrives through evidence arranged by somebody else, and it runs from rage to self-reproach in a single night. Dickens borrows the outline of a tragic jealousy plot, with a trusted informant, a sight through a window and a weapon at a bedroom door, and turns it aside at the last moment.
themes.development: Tackleton plants the idea in Chirp the First and stages the proof in Chirp the Second. In Chirp the Third he finds himself lectured by a man who has thought his way out of it.

themes.name: Seeing and knowing
themes.summary: The blind character hears what the sighted ones miss, and the one scene of plain looking, John at the window, produces a false conclusion. Caleb's word-pictures for Bertha and Tackleton's arranged view for John are versions of the same act: telling someone else what they are looking at.
themes.development: Bertha hears the young man's step in Chirp the Second, and John sees Dot at the window the same evening. In Chirp the Third Bertha asks Dot to say what she sees, and calls the answer her sight restored.

themes.name: Kind lies and kept secrets
themes.summary: Caleb lies to Bertha out of love and Dot hides Edward's return out of loyalty to May, and both concealments do harm before they do any good. The book forgives both, but only after each has been confessed in full.
themes.development: Caleb's question about deceiving Bertha from her cradle begins in Chirp the Second; Dot's secret nearly ends her marriage; both are told on the same morning, one straight after the other.

themes.name: Toys, trade and work
themes.summary: Almost everyone here works for a living: a carrier with two rounds, a toymaker nailing harness onto wooden horses, a doll's dressmaker who cannot see her dolls. Tackleton’s business makes childhood into stock, and Caleb’s room, with dolls graded by class and figures worked by little handles, is a small model of the adult world.
themes.development: The toys are described at length in Chirp the Second, watch the picnic like an audience, and stand run down and staring at the end of that Chirp. The last sentence of the book leaves a single broken toy on the ground.

themes.name: Forgiveness
themes.summary: John forgives Dot before he knows she is innocent: he takes the blame on himself and offers her freedom with his blessing. The later reconciliations, Bertha with her father and everyone with Tackleton, come more quickly and cost the forgiven party less.
themes.development: John's speech to Tackleton is the turning point; Dot asks him not to love her again until he has heard everything; Tackleton is forgiven within five minutes of walking in.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator who talks to the reader, arguing, teasing and admitting to opinions of his own.
techniques.inThisBook: The first page is an argument with the reader about whether the kettle or the cricket began, and the narrator keeps stepping in: he defends Dot’s figure, warns that the reader may learn to hate her, and in the last paragraph turns out to have been in the room watching the dance.

techniques.name: Personification
techniques.definition: Giving human feelings, speech or motives to objects and animals.
techniques.inThisBook: The kettle sulks, dribbles like a drunk and sings a song about the weather; the Hay-maker on the Dutch clock suffers every time it strikes; Boxer is credited with tact towards a blind girl. The house is animated so thoroughly that the Cricket's speaking part in Chirp the Third reads as an extension of the style.

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: A speech habit belonging to one character alone, so that they can be recognised before they are named.
techniques.inThisBook: John is always very near a joke, Tilly makes every noun plural when she repeats adult talk to the baby, Mrs Fielding goes back to the Indigo Trade, and Caleb falls back on a song about a Sparkling Bowl whenever a question gets too close.

techniques.name: Refrain
techniques.definition: A phrase brought back at intervals, so that its meaning shifts with what has happened since.
techniques.inThisBook: Caleb's question, whether he deceived Bertha from her cradle only to break her heart, is spoken once and then read twice more in his face, and Tilly chants a pluralised version of it to the baby. The chirp works the same way, meaning welcome, then warning, then mercy.

techniques.name: Disguise
techniques.definition: A character concealing their identity, so that some people in the story know more than others.
techniques.inThisBook: Edward's white wig and pretended deafness keep the reader as much in the dark as John. Dot knows, and Bertha half hears through it, and the narrator's comments are arranged so that the reader shares John's reading of the window.

techniques.name: Symbolic objects
techniques.definition: An object the narrative comes back to until it stands for the argument itself.
techniques.inThisBook: Dot's little stool, the pipe she fills, the Dutch clock and Tackleton's wedding cake are introduced as household furniture and later carry the state of the marriage. Dot bungles the pipe when she is frightened, John cannot bear to look at the empty stool, and the cake ends up on the Peerybingles' table.

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: A story or figure in which characters stand for ideas and act them out.
techniques.inThisBook: In Chirp the Third the Cricket becomes the Genius of the Hearth, and Household Fairies act out Dot's virtues in a glass, rubbing out the Stranger's shadow whenever it falls. The fairy-tale subtitle is made literal here, and the allegory is kept to John's night of thinking.

quotations.text: The kettle began it! Don’t tell me what Mrs. Peerybingle said. I know better.
quotations.context: The first sentences of the book.
quotations.analysis: The narrator starts with a quarrel over which household noise came first, and conducts it like a witness who will not be contradicted. His 'I know better' comes back in Tackleton's mouth, 'We know better, you know', when he hints that the Peerybingles' happiness is for show, and John's reply is to refuse the phrase.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the First

quotations.text: Oh, Mother Nature, give thy children the true poetry of heart that hid itself in this poor Carrier’s breast—he was but a Carrier, by the way—and we can bear to have them talking prose, and leading lives of prose
quotations.context: The narrator's portrait of John after his first failed attempt at a joke.
quotations.analysis: Dickens uses the old division between poetry and prose to make a point about class: the carrier talks prose and lives a life of prose, and the aside ‘he was but a Carrier, by the way’ mimics a speaker who would look down on him. The sentence is itself an appeal to Nature, so the narrator supplies the poetry that John never gets to the end of a joke to reach.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the First

quotations.text: I did fear once, John; I was very young, you know—that ours might prove to be an ill-assorted marriage, I being such a child, and you more like my guardian than my husband
quotations.context: Dot tells John what the cricket's chirp meant to her when she first came to his house, nearly a year before.
quotations.analysis: Dot introduces the fear as something she once had, and the dash that breaks the sentence suggests it is not quite over. 'More like my guardian than my husband' is the charge John brings against himself in Chirp the Third, so when he decides the marriage was unequal he is finishing a sentence she began here.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the First

quotations.text: Bah! what’s home? … Four walls and a ceiling! (Why don’t you kill that Cricket? I would! I always do. I hate their noise.)
quotations.context: Tackleton invites the Peerybingles to spend an evening with him and May, and John says they keep their wedding day at home.
quotations.analysis: Tackleton's definition of home is the one the book's title exists to answer, and his aside about killing crickets sits in brackets as if it were too obvious to say aloud. The boast comes back at the end, when he admits there is no cricket left on his own hearth, so the insult supplies the terms of his apology.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the First

quotations.text: Oh, Dot! Oh, failing Dot! There is no place for it in all your husband’s visions. Why has its shadow fallen on his hearth?
quotations.context: The close of Chirp the First: John's fireside vision of Dots at every age is joined by a young man's figure at her stool, repeating 'Married! and not to me!'
quotations.analysis: Speaking to Dot as if she were already guilty, the narrator calls her 'failing', a word that prepares the reader to take the next Chirp John's way. The charge comes as questions about a shadow, and a shadow is close to what the young man is: a lover the others believe dead, returned in disguise.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the First

quotations.text: I should have said that Caleb lived here, and his poor Blind Daughter somewhere else—in an enchanted home of Caleb’s furnishing, where scarcity and shabbiness were not, and trouble never entered.
quotations.context: The narrator corrects his opening sentence about where Caleb and his daughter live.
quotations.analysis: Dickens revises himself in mid-paragraph, and the revision splits one address into two houses. The enchanted home is defined by what it lacks, scarcity, shabbiness, trouble, and the next paragraph fills the gap with what Bertha 'never knew': discoloured ceilings, rotting wood, a father going grey in front of her.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Second

quotations.text: For years and years he had never once crossed that threshold at his own slow pace, but with a footfall counterfeited for her ear; and never had he, when his heart was heaviest, forgotten the light tread that was to render hers so cheerful and courageous!
quotations.context: Bertha has described the father she imagines, with a free step and dark hair, and the narrator explains how she came by the picture.
quotations.analysis: Caleb's deception reaches his own body: he has acted a lighter walk for his daughter's ear for years. 'Counterfeited' is a coiner's word, and it makes the kindness a forgery, which is close to how Caleb puts it himself when he confesses that the eyes she trusted were false to her.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Second

quotations.text: Father, I am lonely in the dark. I want my eyes, my patient, willing eyes.
quotations.context: After Tackleton has announced his marriage to May, Bertha sits down beside her father at his workbench.
quotations.analysis: Bertha calls her father her eyes and gives the eyes two virtues that belong to a person, patience and willingness. What she wants is description, and Caleb's answer, that the shed is 'Homely, but very snug', shows him lying to the owner of the eyes in the act of lending them.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Second

quotations.text: Have I deceived her from her cradle, but to break her heart at last?
quotations.context: Bertha has fallen at May's feet and confessed that May's marriage to Tackleton has nearly broken her heart.
quotations.analysis: Caleb's question has the grammar of a prayer, addressed to 'Great Power', and it holds his whole history with Bertha in two clauses. Dickens repeats it twice more as the narrator reads it in Caleb's face, and then Tilly Slowboy chants it to the baby with the nouns made plural, which is how it reaches Tackleton.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Second

quotations.text: He saw them stop, and saw her turn—to have the face, the face he loved so, so presented to his view!—and saw her, with her own hands, adjust the lie upon his head, laughing, as she did it, at his unsuspicious nature!
quotations.context: Tackleton has taken John across the yard to his dark counting-house, whose window looks into the lamplit ware-room.
quotations.analysis: John's evidence is laid out as a series of things 'he saw', and one noun gives the method away: Dot adjusts 'the lie' on the stranger's head. The word is the narrator's, a pun on the false hair and on deceit, and it leaves open, as John cannot, the question of whose lie it is.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Second

quotations.text: When suddenly, the struggling fire illuminated the whole chimney with a glow of light; and the Cricket on the Hearth began to Chirp!
quotations.context: John has taken a loaded gun from the wall and lifted it to beat in the stranger's door.
quotations.analysis: The rescue comes from the fire and a household insect, and the sentence stages it like lighting and sound arriving on cue. The broken-off sentence before 'When suddenly' leaves John's arm in the air, and the capital on 'Chirp' gives the smallest sound in the house the weight of a verdict.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Third

quotations.text: Otherwise I never could have loved her as I did … The Voice, correcting him, said “do.” The Carrier repeated “as I did.” But not firmly.
quotations.context: The Cricket, in fairy shape, repeats what Dot said about loving it, and John answers.
quotations.analysis: The argument of the whole night is conducted over a verb's tense. John puts his love in the past to protect himself, the Cricket moves it into the present, and when John repeats the past tense 'not firmly' the grammar shows the change before he admits it.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Third

quotations.text: I had studied myself; I had had experience of myself; I knew how much I loved her, and how happy I should be … But I had not—I feel it now—sufficiently considered her.
quotations.context: The next morning John tells Tackleton the conclusion he reached during the night.
quotations.analysis: John's three clauses about himself are balanced and practised, and the fourth breaks at a dash, which is where the night's thinking shows. 'Sufficiently considered her' is mild wording for what follows: he blames himself for taking a young woman from her friends to a dull house, and offers to set her free.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Third

quotations.text: The world you live in, heart of mine, doesn’t exist as I have represented it. The eyes you have trusted in have been false to you.
quotations.context: Caleb, with Dot beside him, begins his confession to Bertha on Tackleton's wedding morning.
quotations.analysis: Caleb is exact about the scale of what he did: the whole world she lives in. He calls her 'heart of mine' in the same breath, keeping the tender manner of the fiction while he takes it apart, and 'the eyes you have trusted in' picks up Bertha's own name for him from Chirp the Second.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Third

quotations.text: It is my sight restored. It is my sight! … I have been blind, and now my eyes are open. I never knew him!
quotations.context: Dot has described Caleb to Bertha as he is, an old man worn with care and work.
quotations.analysis: Bertha uses the language of a miraculous cure for an event in which nothing happens to her eyes. What she has gained is an accurate description, supplied by Dot, and Dickens lets her count it as sight; the short last sentence, 'I never knew him', admits what the years of protection cost her.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Third

quotations.text: Now, my dear husband, take me to your heart again! That’s my home, John; and never, never think of sending me to any other!
quotations.context: Dot has told her secret and kept John at arm's length until she has said everything.
quotations.analysis: Dot moves the book's key word: home is John's heart, and she forbids him to send her 'to any other', answering his plan to return her to her parents' house. The doubled 'never, never' closes the doubt she confessed in Chirp the First, when she feared she might not learn to love him.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Third

quotations.text: Friends, one and all, my house is very lonely to-night. I have not so much as a Cricket on my Hearth. I have scared them all away.
quotations.context: Tackleton arrives in person after sending the wedding cake and a parcel of toys to the Peerybingles' party.
quotations.analysis: Tackleton's apology is built from his own boast in Chirp the First: he said he killed crickets, and now reports there are none left in his house. Loneliness is the only reason he gives, and 'I have scared them all away' is honest about his own part in it.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Third

quotations.text: A Cricket sings upon the Hearth; a broken child’s toy lies upon the ground: and nothing else remains.
quotations.context: The last sentences of the book, straight after the dance.
quotations.analysis: Having been at the party all along, the narrator is left alone in the present tense with two objects. The cricket is the one sound left over from the first page, and setting a broken toy beside it, in a book full of Caleb's toys, lets the ending read as the close of a children's game as well as of a story.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg eBook 20795, Chirp the Third

timeline.label: Dickens born in Portsmouth
timeline.detail: Born on 7 February at Landport, the son of a clerk in the Navy Pay Office.

timeline.label: A Christmas Carol published
timeline.detail: The first of the five Christmas books, issued by Chapman and Hall in December.

timeline.label: The Chimes published
timeline.detail: The second Christmas book, written in Genoa during Dickens's year in Italy and more openly political than the first.

timeline.label: A periodical called The Cricket is proposed and dropped
timeline.detail: Dickens suggested to John Forster a cheap weekly under that title, with the cricket as the voice of the fireside; the idea went into the Christmas book instead.

timeline.label: The Cricket on the Hearth published
timeline.detail: Bradbury and Evans issued it shortly before Christmas, dedicated to Lord Jeffrey and illustrated by five artists; the title page is dated 1846.

timeline.label: On the London stage within weeks
timeline.detail: Albert Smith's adaptation, prepared with Dickens's agreement, opened at the Lyceum in December, and rival versions followed at other theatres.

timeline.label: Dickens edits the Daily News
timeline.detail: Bradbury and Evans backed the new Liberal daily, which first appeared on 21 January; Dickens gave up the editorship within weeks.

timeline.label: The Battle of Life published
timeline.detail: The fourth Christmas book, another domestic story with no ghosts in it.

timeline.label: Dickens reads the Cricket in public
timeline.detail: He read it at Birmingham Town Hall in the last week of December, alongside A Christmas Carol, in the first public readings he gave.

timeline.label: Boucicault's Dot opens in New York
timeline.detail: Dion Boucicault's adaptation gave Joseph Jefferson the part of Caleb Plummer, which became one of his best-known roles.

timeline.label: Dickens dies at Gad's Hill
timeline.detail: He died on 9 June, three months after his farewell reading in London.

timeline.label: Goldmark's opera Das Heimchen am Herd
timeline.detail: Karl Goldmark's opera based on the story was first performed at the Vienna Court Opera.

places.name: Whitefriars, off Fleet Street
places.note: Bradbury and Evans's printing works; the 1846 title page gives the publishers' address as 90 Fleet Street and Whitefriars.

places.name: Lyceum Theatre, Wellington Street
places.note: Where Albert Smith's stage version opened in December 1845.

places.name: Birmingham Town Hall
places.note: Dickens read the Cricket here in December 1853.

criticalViews.position: The home as a sacred space
criticalViews.summary: The Cricket is often read as the plainest statement in the Christmas books of the Victorian ideal of the hearth: the fireside is an altar, the wife its presiding spirit, and domestic sounds carry moral truth. The Cricket's speech to John in Chirp the Third puts the idea almost in those words.
criticalViews.counter: The book also shows a home being described into existence, as Caleb does for Bertha, and it makes the whole household vanish in its last paragraph, leaving the narrator alone with a broken toy.

criticalViews.position: A jealousy plot turned to comedy
criticalViews.summary: The middle of the book borrows the machinery of tragic jealousy: a trusted informant, a sight through a window that seems to prove betrayal, a husband with a weapon outside a bedroom door. On this reading the Cricket's intervention and John's self-blame are Dickens's deliberate refusal of the tragic ending.
criticalViews.counter: The comparison can make John sound more dangerous than the book allows. His first act after seeing the window is to shield Dot from Tackleton's eyes, and the scene with the gun lasts a few paragraphs of a long night.

criticalViews.position: A story made for the stage
criticalViews.summary: The Cricket was adapted for the London stage within weeks of publication and held it for decades, with Joseph Jefferson's Caleb Plummer the best-known American version. A disguise, a scene at a lit window, a recognition and a closing dance give it the shape of a domestic melodrama.
criticalViews.counter: Much of the book's effect depends on a narrator who argues with the reader, misleads about Dot and finally vanishes with his characters, and that voice has no place in a theatre.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens present John Peerybingle's jealousy, and why does it not end in violence?
essayQuestions.focus: Jealousy, evidence and the Cricket's intervention
plan: Start with Tackleton's hints in Chirp the First and the way they stay in John's slow mind, alongside Tilly's nonsense, 'like a lesson'.
Read the window scene closely: the repeated 'he saw', and the narrator's word 'lie' for the white wig.
Examine the gun and the chirp: what exactly stops John, and why Dickens makes it the memory of Dot's voice.
Show the night's reasoning becoming self-blame in the speech to Tackleton, especially 'sufficiently considered her'.
Decide whether John's forgiveness before he knows the truth matters more than the revelation that follows.

essayQuestions.question: 'A fairy tale of home.' How far does The Cricket on the Hearth question the home it celebrates?
plan: Define the home of Chirp the First through its sounds and habits: kettle, clock, pipe and stool.
Set Tackleton's 'four walls and a ceiling' against it, and his later admission that he has no cricket.
Use Caleb's two houses, the cracked shed and the enchanted home, to show a home made out of description.
Consider the unequal marriages, and Mrs Fielding's view that the least loving matches are the happiest.
End on the vanishing last paragraph and decide whether it confirms the fairy tale or reminds the reader that it is one.

essayQuestions.question: How does Dickens use Caleb and Bertha Plummer to show a kind deception?
plan: Begin with the narrator's correction: Caleb lives in one house and Bertha in another.
Analyse the blue coat and the counterfeited footfall as lies told through objects and through the body.
Trace the damage, from Bertha's love for the benefactor Caleb invented to her confession at May's feet.
Read the confession scene, including Dot's description of Caleb and Bertha's claim that her sight is restored.
Compare Dot's secret and weigh whether the book finally approves of either concealment.

discussionQuestions: Tackleton says his match with May and the Peerybingles' marriage are just alike. What does the book offer for and against him?
This is a Christmas book set at the end of January. Does anything in it depend on Christmas?
Was Caleb wrong to describe the world to Bertha as he did, and what else could he have done?
The narrator encourages the reader to suspect Dot. Is that fair to the reader, or to her?
Tackleton changes his mind in an afternoon. Do you believe him?
What does Bertha mean when she says she is not blind any longer?

related.why: The first Christmas book, and the model the Cricket moves away from: a miser converted at Christmas against a jealous husband at the end of January.
The Christmas book Dickens wrote the year before, where church bells do the work the cricket does here.
The last of the Christmas books, in which another household spirit offers a bargain about memory.
The tragic version of John Peerybingle's night: a trusted informant, an arranged sight and a husband who does not stop.
The Cricket in one volume with A Christmas Carol, The Chimes and The Haunted Man.
